title: Build a Live Set
blurb: Turn finished loops into a set you can perform: sections on pads, chained patterns, and transitions you have actually rehearsed.

steps.title: Decide what a pad means
body: Before touching the unit, decide how the set is laid out: one pad per section, one pad per stem, or patterns for the arrangement and pads for one-shots.
Mixing those approaches mid-set is what makes live sets fall apart — you reach for a pad and get the wrong kind of thing.
A workable default: bottom row for section loops, second row for drum one-shots you drop over the top, upper rows for vocals, stabs, and FX.
Write the layout down. You will not remember it under stage lights.
steps.checkpoint: You can say what every pad in the bank does without playing it.
steps.tip: Keep the same layout across every track in the set. Consistency beats cleverness once you are performing.

steps.title: Print your sections
body: Resample each section down to a single pad, so playing it live is one hit rather than four hands' worth of juggling.
Trim every section to loop seamlessly and check them at the tempo you will actually play at.
Keep the unprinted parts in another bank in case you need to rebuild a section later.
Set the loop and pad-play behaviour so a section holds until you change it, instead of stopping the moment you lift your finger.
steps.checkpoint: Each section pad loops cleanly on its own and drops in on the downbeat.
steps.tip: Print sections a little longer than you think you need. Trimming a long loop live is impossible; extending a short one is worse.

steps.title: Chain patterns for the parts you do not want to babysit
body: Anything with a fixed arrangement — an intro that always runs eight bars, a fill before the drop — belongs in a pattern chain rather than in your hands.
Record those as patterns and chain them in playing order, then keep your hands free for the parts you want to perform.
The Pattern Sequencer guide covers recording and chaining in detail if you have not done it yet.
Leave the sections you improvise over as loose pads. A set that is entirely sequenced is a playback, not a performance.
steps.checkpoint: The fixed parts play themselves in order while your hands stay on the pads.
steps.tip: Decide deliberately which half is sequenced and which half is played. Drifting into all-sequenced happens one convenient decision at a time.

steps.title: Rehearse the transitions, not the loops
body: Loops are the easy part — they already sound good. Sets fall over in the four bars where one section becomes another.
Practise only the changeovers: play the last two bars of one section and the first two of the next, then stop, then again.
Use a filter sweep or a delay throw on the Bus FX as the transition rather than a hard cut, and print the FX if you want it identical every time.
Count the change in out loud until it is automatic.
steps.checkpoint: You can move between any two adjacent sections on the downbeat, ten times in a row, without looking.
steps.tip: This is the same skill the Pad Transitions lesson drills: knowing where your hand is going before it goes there.

steps.title: Build a way out of trouble
body: Keep one pad holding a simple drum loop at set tempo. If anything goes wrong, that pad buys you eight bars to fix it.
Know how to mute everything in one move and how to get back to a known-good state.
Run the whole set start to finish without stopping, including the bits you know you can play. That full pass is the rehearsal — the rest is practice.
Back the project up to your computer before you take it anywhere.
steps.checkpoint: You have played the set end to end, once, without stopping to fix anything.
steps.tip: Something will go wrong live. The difference between a good and a bad set is entirely in how boring the recovery looks from the audience.
